doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

title: Jazz Institute versus the college, and reaching audiences
summary: He compares freedom at the institute with college layers, and discusses marketing the blues festival versus West Coast jazz festivals.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: many layers that you deal with when you’re at the college. You know there’s many different layers. Whereas at the Jazz Institute there’s none of those layers you know. You can pretty much do things exactly — people get paid exactly how you need to get — you know all those things. At the college it’s a whole different thing as you well know. So again you have to adapt, you have to adapt to the circumstances, which is what we’ve always tried to do but I can say that I feel pretty good that we’ve not made compromises and I’m proud of that without events. I don’t feel like we’ve ever made compromises to try to make more money or to try to bring in more people or whatever the case may be. We’ve always just tried — my thing has been is that there’s enough of an audience out there, especially where I am in L.A. and San Diego — there’s enough of an audience out there that will support what you’re doing, you just have to — you just have to find out — to get them to listen to the radio or to attend the event, or whatever it is that you’re trying to get them to do. I don’t have visions of — I don’t have visions that there’s — like for example in San Diego I’m sure that a huge percentage of people who like jazz or even on a very periphery like jazz, they know our radio station exists. We don’t necessarily have to go find some unknown thousands of potential audience out there that doesn’t know we exist. We have to get the people who are our audience to support the radio station during fundraisers and things like that. And just like any public radio station, classical music or jazz, either one, the percentage of people who donate during membership drives is a teeny-tiny percentage of the listeners. I mean it’s like I don’t know four percent or something. It’s a tiny percentage. If we could get half of the people who listen on a regular basis just to become a member we wouldn’t have a care in the world for years. But it’s never been that way and I don’t have any visions that we’re going to necessarily be able to change that, but you just keep trying to get that percentage to go up. And it’s the same with events. You know I don’t go buy billboards on Sunset Boulevard when we’re doing a jazz festi — a straight ahead jazz festival because I’m spending money to reach an audience that’s not going to come no matter what. So I always try to focus more on getting the message to the audience that’s there, not to try to — and again if our, maybe our purpose is to do something where we’re trying to enlarge the audience and then we might do different things. But see for the Long Beach Blues Festival that I did for years and years, now that was a little bit of a different animal, because the Long Beach Blues Festival did attract and could attract and appeal to a more commercial audience or a different audience depending on who you had as headliners and people attending. So yeah, we’d buy bus placards sometimes or whatever you call those things on the side of a bus. And we would take out full page ads in the L.A. Times. I would never take out a full page ad in the L.A. Times for, you know, a West Coast jazz festival that featured Shorty Rogers and Gerry Mulligan and Howard Rumsey and so on and so

forth. But for the blues festival, yeah, because we would have, you know, B.B. King and you know people like that. And they appeal — so you approach it a different way. Blues festival we’d get 20,000 people a day. Again, I never had any visions that our West Coast Jazz Festival would get 20,000 people. I knew that if we could draw a couple thousand people collectively over the four days or three days or whatever it is, that it would all work out just great. So I don’t want to paint the wrong picture. It’s not that I don’t realize the importance of developing the audience and expanding the audience, we certainly do try to do those things. But there’s a lot of people doing that that I’m sure is doing a good job with it so you know we try to give them something good that as they expand that audience they have somewhere to send them.
We do our part with that, certainly with the radio station I mean you know expanding the audiences.
